record.original_question: Can one develop computationally tractable topological and numerical tools that decide, a priori, whether a given stabilization problem admits a solution, with checks that are easier than brute-force numerical experimentation and that still provide certificates of accuracy when the control law or vector field data are noisy, approximate, or experimentally obtained? Computational homology and topological data analysis are proposed as possible ingredients in such certified decision procedures.

evidence.quote: Numerical tools: This line of work aims to provide necessary and sufficient conditions so that one can assess—a priori—if a stabilization problem has a solution. Clearly, these conditions must be easier to check than a brute force numerical experiment for this to be of practical value.
computational tools must be able to provide certificates of accuracy

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let M be a smooth manifold and let f: M × U → TM be a control system, i.e. for each control value u ∈ U ⊂ R^m, f(·,u) is a smooth vector field on M, and let x* ∈ M be a target equilibrium. A (continuous, possibly time-varying or discontinuous) feedback law k: M → U is said to stabilize the system at x* if the closed-loop vector field X_k(x) := f(x,k(x)) renders x* (globally or locally) asymptotically stable. Assume the data (f, and possibly k) are only known approximately: one has access to an approximation f̃ with ‖f̃ − f‖ ≤ ε in some appropriate norm on a compact region K ⊂ M, possibly arising from experimental measurements.

Develop a computationally tractable decision procedure with the following properties:

(1) Given (M, f, x*) (or its approximation f̃ together with the noise bound ε), the procedure outputs in finite time either
   (a) a certificate that no continuous stabilizing feedback exists for the system at x*, or
   (b) a certificate that a stabilizing feedback exists, together with quantitative robustness margins valid for every system within the ε-ball around f̃.

(2) The complexity of the procedure must be strictly lower than that of brute-force simulation over a dense grid of initial conditions and candidate feedbacks.

(3) The certificates produced must be sound under the noise model: if the procedure certifies (a) or (b) for f̃, then the same conclusion holds for the true f provided ‖f̃ − f‖ ≤ ε.

In particular, design and analyze such a procedure built from computational homology and topological-data-analysis invariants (e.g. persistent homology of sublevel sets of candidate Lyapunov functions, topological obstructions to continuous sections of sphere bundles such as Brockett-type degree/index conditions, Conley-index computations on cubical or simplicial approximations of the flow), and prove its correctness, soundness with respect to the ε-noise model, and a complexity bound demonstrating tractability.
artifact.category_tag: Certified numerical tools for nonlinear stabilization
artifact.status_search_result: The question is a broad research-direction proposal calling for certified, topology-based numerical procedures that decide a priori solvability of nonlinear stabilization problems under noisy data. While there is active work on computational Conley index, persistent-homology-based Lyapunov function construction, and SOS/SDP certificates for stability, no general procedure meeting all the stated requirements (a-priori decision, noise certificates, sub-brute-force complexity) is known. The problem appears open.
